papers.title: Central Limit Theorems and Network-Free Inference for Heterogeneous Spatial Autoregressions on Sparse Graphons
papers.summary: Network dependence is widely regarded as a fundamental obstacle to inference: outcomes linked through a graph are not independent, the graph is rarely observed in full, and models for how dependence propagates are easily misspecified. We show that for a broad class of responses generated through a random network, the obstacle is smaller than it appears. We study a heterogeneous spatial autoregression on a sparse graphon, in which each node's response is a weighted average of its neighbors' responses with a node-specific, nonparametric coefficient plus a node-specific input, and we prove that sample means and smooth functions of vector means are asymptotically Gaussian down to average degree nearly logarithmic in the population size, allowing unbounded graphons with hubs and heavy-tailed inputs. The limiting variance interpolates exactly between two regimes according to the sampling fraction. When the observed nodes are a vanishing fraction of the population, the variance is the marginal variance of the response, the ordinary sample variance is consistent, and the usual $t$-interval is valid with no knowledge of the network. The proof averages over the graph rather than conditioning on it, isolating the behavior of the response through an exact identity for resolvents of Markov kernels and controlling the network noise by an Efron-Stein inequality; neither step requires the walk-by-walk covariance bounds of fixed-network analyses. Consequences for regression with node-level and network-derived covariates are derived.

papers.title: An ODE-based Sampler for Discrete Diffusion Models
papers.summary: The marginals of a continuous diffusion model can be reproduced by a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), known as the probability flow ODE, which provides a foundation for accelerated sampling and consistency distillation. In this paper we address the question whether an analogous formulation exists for discrete diffusion models and answer it affirmatively by introducing exponential residual flows (ERFs). Our framework augments the discrete state with a continuous residual variable for each token and position. These residuals evolve deterministically according to piecewise-defined ODEs whose vector fields depend on the current discrete state and the forward and backward rate matrices of the prescribed diffusion model. The discrete state changes whenever a residual reaches zero. We prove that this construction preserves the marginals of the original diffusion. We derive a practical discretization of our sampler and specialize it to masked and uniform diffusion. The deterministic trajectories of ERFs support consistency distillation and yield empirical improvements over previous approaches across a variety of benchmarks including code and text generation tasks.

papers.title: Self-regularization and structural adaptation of NPMLE for Gaussian mixture models in all dimensions
papers.summary: We establish structural properties of the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) for $d$-dimensional Gaussian mixtures whose means lie in a hypercube. We show that, with high probability, the NPMLE based on $n$ independent observations self-regularizes by fitting a mixture model with $O((\frac{\log n}{\log\log n})^d)$ components, achieving the optimal model complexity without explicit model selection. Furthermore, the NPMLE exhibits a structural adaptation property: For data drawn from a finite mixture, the number of fitted components is bounded in probability as $n\to\infty$. Our proof applies a multivariate Jensen-type bound to control the typical number of critical points of the KKT function associated with the first-order optimality conditions. The key step is to lower bound its gradient norm uniformly on complex spheres. We establish this lower bound by decomposing the KKT function into an empirical fluctuation term and a relative density estimation error term, combining small-ball probability estimates for the former with polynomial approximation and Hellinger error bounds for the latter.

papers.title: A case study of hybrid statistical models for analyzing spatio-temporal effects in historical map series of Donau-Ries county
papers.summary: This case study compares generalized linear models, generalized additive models, and semi-structured deep distributional regression for analyzing settlement patterns in historical land-cover maps. Using four reference years for Donau-Ries county (Landkreis Donau-Ries) in southern Germany, we quantify how distances to agricultural areas, forests, and rivers relate to residential presence, and we evaluate predictive performance through spatial block cross-validation. Classical models yield stable and interpretable distance effects, whereas the semi-structured framework improves prediction once local image context is included. The analysis illustrates a practical trade-off between interpretability, accuracy, and robustness when interpretable covariates are combined with deep components in spatio-temporal data analysis.
papers.comment: 28 pages, 8 figures. Preprint prepared for Communications in Statistics: Case Studies, Data Analysis and Applications

papers.title: Numerical Integration on Bounded Domains via Learned Reflected Diffusions
papers.summary: We study high-dimensional integration on bounded convex domains. Given a non-negative integrand $r$, the goal is to estimate $Z=\int_{D}r(x)\,\mathrm dx$ on $D\subset\mathbb R^d$. Standard Quasi-Monte Carlo does not adapt its evaluation points to the integrand, while effective importance sampling requires a proposal that captures its concentration. Learned diffusion samplers can supply such a proposal, but existing methods are formulated on $\mathbb R^d$ and do not respect the domain constraint $x\in D$. We instead build the proposal from reflected dynamics that stay in $D$ by construction. A reflected diffusion progressively transforms the target distribution toward the uniform distribution on $D$, and a neural score model is trained to reverse this process. A change-of-measure formula for reflected diffusions yields a training objective without additional boundary terms and an unbiased importance-sampling estimator of $Z$. For non-smooth integrands, where reparameterization gradients may be undefined or uninformative, we derive a REINFORCE estimator of the training gradient using Gaussian proposal densities before reflection, without evaluating reflected transition densities or differentiating $r$. We evaluate on numerous synthetic targets and real-world problems, demonstrating strong performance of the proposed method, as well as favorable scaling with the dimension of the problem and the number of points used for the Monte Carlo estimate.

papers.title: Weak Factor Recovery in Sparse Bayesian Factor Models under Exchangeable Shrinkage Process Prior
papers.summary: Sparse Bayesian factor models provide a flexible framework for learning low-dimensional latent structure in multivariate data, but inference on the number of active factors remains challenging when some factors are weak or highly sparse. We study weak factor recovery under a variance based exchangeable shrinkage process (ESP) prior. We derive the posterior factor activation mechanism and show that, conditional on the global and local shrinkage parameters, activation is governed by the standardised loading energy together with the ESP prior activation odds. This yields an explicit activation boundary and clarifies how signal strength, sparsity, the number of observed variables, and the truncation level affect recovery. Simulation experiments show a clear transition between shrinkage and recovery around this boundary and demonstrate that sparsity can substantially affect activation even when raw loading energy is held fixed. They further show that factor activation and recovery of the relative loading pattern across variables can behave differently. These results clarify when weak latent factors become difficult to distinguish from redundant components under ESP shrinkage.

papers.title: Rural Readiness: Domain Generalization with Adversarially Chosen Domains
papers.summary: Predictive models trained at well-resourced data-rich institutions often fail when deployed in new populations. Motivated by the goal of building clinical diagnosis and decision-making algorithms for data-scarce rural populations using the general knowledge learned from data-rich hospitals, we formulate the fundamental question of \emph{domain generalization with adversarially chosen domains}, which asks a learner to perform on any unseen target domain nearly as well as the worst hypothesis consistent with the evidence from the observed source domains. Assuming only that the hypothesis class contains a "universal" predictor with small error on all $k$ source domains, we characterize the sample complexity of this objective up to logarithmic factors. Letting $d$ denote the VC dimension of the hypothesis class, we find, somewhat surprisingly, that the sample complexity reduces significantly from $Ω(dk)$ to $O(d)$ under a small relaxation of the learning goal in which, roughly speaking, we allow the learned model to compete with hypotheses that perform well on 99% instead of 100% of the source domains. By applying this insight to the meta-distributional setting, in which source domains are selected according to a distribution on distributions, we obtain a corresponding improvement over known sample complexity upper bounds. We also study the effect of data access to the target domain and show that a small labeled sample from the target domain does not improve the worst-case sample complexity on the source domains.

papers.title: Finite-Sample LTI System Identification from a Misspecified Finite Model Set
papers.summary: We consider the problem of finite-sample identification of an unknown LTI system from a finite hypothesis class. In contrast to existing results that assume the hypothesis class contains the true system, we consider the misspecified setting, where the true system does not belong to the hypothesis class. We first characterize the resulting estimation target and its dependence on the data-generation scheme. We then establish a finite-sample lower bound on the failure probability that any identification algorithm must incur. Finally, we analyze the robustness of an existing exponential weighting-based identification algorithm to the misspecification and derive a finite-sample upper bound on its failure probability. Our results illustrate when using a misspecified finite hypothesis class can provide an advantage over identification without prior knowledge of the candidate systems.
category_names_zh: eess.SY (系统与控制理论 (Systems and Control))

papers.title: Conformal ordering: Distribution-free predictive inference for orders and rank
papers.summary: We study distribution-free predictive inference for the ordering and ranking of multiple unobserved outcomes. Although numerous methods, such as conformal prediction, have been developed for prediction and predictive inference of unobserved outcomes, extending them to provide inference for the ordering of multiple outcomes with an interpretable guarantee is not straightforward. To this end, we develop a framework and methodology for uncertainty quantification in predictive ordering. Our approach begins by reformulating the problem of determining an ordering among multiple objects as a graph inference problem. Our method adopts a multiple-testing-inspired approach and constructs an uncertainty graph, where each edge represents a confidently inferred pairwise ordering. We develop a distribution-free procedure for constructing a consistent uncertainty graph while controlling either the family-wise error rate or the false discovery rate. Moreover, we show that the resulting graphs naturally yield risk-controlling prediction intervals for the ranks of the outcomes. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed procedure achieves the target guarantees tightly while maintaining reasonable power and prediction-interval widths.

papers.title: Optimal Neural Estimation for High-Dimensional Nonparametric Regression under Multisource Covariate Shift
papers.summary: We study high-dimensional nonparametric regression under multisource covariate shift, where $\mathrm J$ sources of training data share a common regression function but differ in their covariate distributions, sample sizes, and noise variances. Our goal is to combine these sources to estimate the regression function accurately under a target covariate distribution. We propose an oracle weighted neural estimator and establish its minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors through matching upper and lower bounds. The resulting rate is $\mathsf n_{\rm eff}^{-2p/(2p+K)}$, where $p$ and $K$ denote the effective smoothness and dimension of the regression function, and the effective sample size is \begin{align} \mathsf n_{\rm eff} =\sum_{j=1}^{\mathrm J} \frac{n_j}{(1+σ_{ρ,j})σ_{ε,j}^{2}}. \nonumber \end{align} Here, $n_j$ is the sample size of source $j$, $σ_{ε,j}^{2}$ is its noise variance, and $σ_{ρ,j}$ controls the deviation between the covariate distribution of source $j$ and the target covariate distribution. We also develop an adaptive procedure that requires no knowledge of source noise variances or covariate-shift parameters. Under suitable conditions, this procedure attains the oracle minimax rate up to logarithmic factors.

papers.title: posterior-landscape: morphological feature finding in two-dimensional probability densities
papers.summary: We present posterior-landscape, a Python framework to identify and characterize morphological features in two-dimensional probability densities. The framework combines concepts from topological data analysis, statistical density-ridge estimation, and scale-space image analysis. It extracts localized concentrations, valleys, ridges, and changes of slope; for Bayesian reconstructions, it propagates uncertainty in feature recovery, geometry, and correspondence across posteriors. The framework also connects two-dimensional structures to features in one-dimensional marginals, and quantifies their correlation with other inferred parameters. We validate the method on controlled densities, and demonstrate its use on gravitational-wave population reconstructions, where it provides a systematic way to identify and interpret population features and assess which ones carry information relevant for cosmology. The resulting catalogues also offer a common morphological representation for future comparisons between predictions and population reconstructions.

papers.title: Reframing Spatial Uncertainty Visualisation with a Layered Grammar of Graphics
papers.summary: Communicating both estimated values and their associated uncertainties presents a particular challenge in spatial visualisation because spatial coordinates already occupy the primary visual channels, leaving relatively few channels available for encoding uncertainty alongside the estimated values. A range of visualisation techniques has been developed to address this challenge, including bivariate choropleth maps, pixel maps, and glyph maps. However, existing implementations typically treat these techniques as dedicated visualisations rather than expressing them through the composable elements of a grammar of graphics. We reframe uncertainty visualisation as an extension of the layered grammar of graphics, allowing uncertainty-specific representations to be composed, customised, and extended alongside other graphical components. We demonstrate this perspective by integrating uncertainty visualisation into the layered architecture of ggplot2, accommodating these techniques while also motivating new approaches such as the dual map for selective attention between estimated values and their associated uncertainties. We implement the framework in the R package ggincerta and demonstrate its application through three case studies.

papers.title: Statistical Analysis of Synthetic Data with Verification: A Linear Regression Framework
papers.summary: Synthetic data are widely used for training modern AI systems. However, their statistical understanding remains limited. It is well recognized in statistics that repeated self-training on synthetic data can amplify errors inherited from pre-trained models, leading to model collapse. Verification plays a crucial role in selecting high-quality synthetic data to help prevent model collapse and improve model performance. We study verified self-training in a linear regression framework, where a pre-trained estimator generates synthetic data with injected generation noise and a verifier selects samples according to a verification threshold. Post-training on the accepted samples updates either all coordinates (full fine-tuning) or only an active subset (partial fine-tuning). Our analysis reveals three potentially counterintuitive effects. We establish that tighter verification does not always lead to lower prediction risk. We also find that a suitable level of injected generation noise can reduce prediction risk, while excessive noise can increase it. Moreover, full and partial fine-tuning can respond differently to the same verification rule, since pre-training error in the frozen coordinates affects both sample selection and post-training risk. We analyze these effects by deriving finite sample risk bounds for four separate regimes determined by the relative scales of the verification threshold, generation noise, and pre-training error. The bounds precisely characterize how verification affects prediction risk across these regimes. In particular, we quantify how the generation noise, the effective accepted sample size, and the covariance of the accepted covariates affect prediction risk. The analysis extends to iterative verified full fine-tuning, where sufficiently tight verification reduces the initial error contribution at a geometric rate.

papers.title: Conformal Annotation with Randomized Expert Review: Application to Online Cell-Type Labeling
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) models can accelerate cell-type annotation in digital pathology, but safely scaling their use requires determining, with error control, which model-generated labels can be accepted without expert review. This is challenging in evolving workflows because cell morphology and type composition may change across tissue regions and slides, making one-time calibration unreliable. We propose Conformal Annotation with Randomized Expert review under Distribution shift (CARED), a distribution-free framework that leverages randomized expert audit to achieve long-run error control for AI-assisted annotation under distribution shift. For each incoming batch, CARED uniformly selects a subset of cases for expert review and uses the acquired labels to calibrate later decisions. Among unreviewed cases, CARED determines a subset of them to safely skip expert labeling, while suggesting candidate labels for the others for downstream resolution. We prove that this workflow provides long-run control of cumulative error over both the full stream and the cells outside of the audit sample, without stationarity or exchangeability assumptions. We further enhance the framework by introducing class-conditional guarantees to ensure error control within important but rare cell types, together with a utility module to target more automatic resolutions, smaller candidate sets, and greater biological coherence, without compromising validity. Experiments on pancreas, lung, and ovary annotation streams, together with a stream constructed from real expert annotations, show that CARED controls the cumulative errors while a substantial fraction of cells (up to 70%) bypass expert review.

papers.title: New hierarchical matrices for fast kernel matrix-vector products with Applications to Gaussian processes and kernel ridge regression
papers.summary: This article presents two new multilevel hierarchical matrices to perform fast kernel matrix-vector products in $d$ dimensions $(d>1)$, namely $\mathcal{H}_{hw}^{\prime}$, $\mathcal{H}_{hw}^{\prime \prime}$. We introduce a novel hybrid weak admissibility condition to construct these hierarchical matrices. More precisely, at coarser levels of the tree (i.e., larger blocks), we use a weak admissibility condition, wherein \textbf{far-field} and \textbf{vertex-sharing} clusters are considered admissible, while at the finer levels (i.e., smaller blocks), the \textbf{adjacent} clusters are treated as admissible. The admissible blocks at coarser levels of $\mathcal{H}_{hw}^{\prime}$ and $\mathcal{H}_{hw}^{\prime \prime}$ are represented using semi-nested and fully nested bases, respectively. In both hierarchical matrices, the finer levels at which adjacent clusters are treated as admissible are constructed in a non-nested fashion. Thus, they can be viewed as a hybrid of $\mathcal{H}$ and $\mathcal{H}^2$ matrices. We use adaptive cross approximation (ACA) and nested cross approximation (NCA) to construct non-nested and nested bases, respectively. The fast matrix-vector products are performed using the proposed hierarchical matrix formats. To evaluate the performance and usefulness of the proposed hierarchical matrices, we conduct some numerical experiments. The numerical results show that they outperform their uniform admissibility counterparts in terms of storage and matrix-vector product cost, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed hybrid formats. We also show that the proposed formats are competitive with the standard (or strong) admissibility-based $\mathcal{H}^2$-matrices. Furthermore, we showcase some interesting applications of the proposed hierarchical matrices.

papers.title: Homogeneity Pursuit of Panel Data with Sparsity
papers.summary: In panel data analysis, studying individual attributes is important for both methodological development and practical applications. Homogeneity in individual attributes and sparsity in coefficients are therefore important topics, as they help uncover relationships among individuals and identify the truly relevant covariates. However, many existing approaches do not explicitly exploit the potential grouping information contained in separately fitted individual-level penalized estimators to identify latent groups. To address this gap, we propose a hierarchical group recovery approach based on sparse initial estimation to jointly identify latent groups and sparse parameter structures in panel data. We first introduce a basic version that can efficiently identify homogeneity and sparsity. Based on this basic version, we further introduce a local search step to improve the performance of our method. Compared with existing methods, our approach shows the best overall performance when jointly considering estimation accuracy and computational efficiency. The simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness and advantages of our approach over existing approaches. We further apply the proposed approach to a real dataset to show its practical applicability.

papers.title: Understanding axial attention in TSFMs through single location regression
papers.summary: Recent advances in Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) increasingly rely on axial attention mechanisms, but despite their empirical success, the theoretical properties of axial attention remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we extend the Single Location Regression framework introduced in Marion et al. [2025] to 2D structured data, in order to study sparse information settings where a target depends on a small number of tokens. We formulate an analytically tractable axial attention-type predictor and rigorously analyze its statistical properties and training dynamics. We prove that under a specific asymptotic regime and with knowledge of the underlying oracle parameters, our predictor achieves Bayes optimality, whereas a class of semi-linear simplifications strictly fails to do so, underlining the role of the inner non-linearity. We prove that for a specific temperature scaling, Projected Gradient Descent converges globally to the optimal oracle parameters. Extensive numerical experiments validate our theoretical findings and highlight the critical role of inverse temperature scheduling in empirical convergence.

papers.title: Hidden Disparities in Ranking: Category-Aware Fairness via Distributional Stability
papers.summary: We study the problem of fair ranking in recommender systems. We provide a formal probabilistic framework in which ranking policies are distributions over permutations, and the utility of a user is the exposure given to the items they interact with, relative to that of an ideal ranking. We consider utility parity across user groups, as well as its category-aware refinement, conditional utility parity, which requires parity within each category of items. Following a recent view of fairness as distributional stability, we show that both criteria are equivalent to the stability of the utility under changes in the composition of user groups. Optimizing over mixtures of ranking policies leads to a second-order cone program, for which we provide generalization bounds. A numerical study validates our theoretical findings.

papers.title: Beyond $χ^2$: Ensemble null tests for reliable scientific discovery
papers.summary: Unrecognized systematic errors can survive standard checks and undermine scientific discoveries. Null tests and experimental controls can expose these failures, but averaging measurements or reducing them to scalar statistics can hide important structure. We propose ensemble null tests that compare multivariate distributions with references from observations or simulations. We demonstrate their benefits across science. In cosmic microwave background simulations, they detect systematic effects missed by conventional $χ^2$ tests. In Gaia data, they detect velocity asymmetry as sensitively as an informed search. In a CRISPR screen, they expose a control mismatch in DNA damage and reveal which cellular profiles drive it. As scientific datasets grow, ensemble testing turns repeated measurements into a broader search for unknown unknowns, strengthening the empirical foundation for scientific discovery.
category_names_zh: astro-ph.CO (宇宙学与河外天体物理)

papers.title: Closing the Log Gap: Minimax-Optimal Regret for Episodic RL
papers.summary: In this paper, we study the regret minimization problem in episodic tabular MDPs. Our algorithm achieves the first expected regret bound scaling as $\sqrt{H^3 S A K}$ for sufficiently large $K$, where $H$ is the episode length, $K$ is the number of episodes, and $S$ and $A$ are the numbers of states and actions, respectively. Our method is the first to match the minimax lower bound \emph{without extra polylog factors}. We introduce a variant of UCBVI which does not maintain strictly optimistic estimates, and uses MOSS-style exploration bonuses whose logarithmic terms adapt to both visit counts and estimated variances. A key challenge is controlling the propagation of errors caused by under-optimism, which we accomplish in an occupancy-weighted way, avoiding logarithmic overhead that would be incurred by uniform-over-rows concentration. Our analysis develops time-uniform and variance-aware concentration bounds that may be of independent interest. As a corollary we also develop an algorithm for $(\varepsilon, δ)$-PAC best-policy identification, which is the first to match the $Ω\big(H^3 SA\log(\frac{1}δ)\varepsilon^{-2}\big)$ minimax lower bound up to constants in some regimes.

papers.title: Fisher Contrastive Learning to Mitigate Feature Suppression: A Case Study in Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia Diagnosis
papers.summary: Self-supervised contrastive learning (SSCL) learns representations by contrasting augmented views of the same sample, but it can exhibit feature suppression, where dominant or easy-to-learn factors suppress other class-relevant signals, degrading the performance of representations, particularly in high-dimensional data with heterogeneous features. We introduce Fisher Contrastive Learning (FCL), which uses a regularized Fisher trace criterion to address feature suppression. FCL learns embeddings by maximizing the discriminative strength of Fisher discriminant functions, producing representations that preserve class-relevant information implied by the augmentation process. We prove that the representations learned by FCL could alleviate the feature suppression effects. We demonstrate FCL on simulated benchmarks designed to induce feature suppression and on a real-world biomedical application, pretraining on large white blood cell microscopy image dataset and transfer learning for diagnosis of acute promyelocytic leukemia in an external cohort. In all experiments, FCL outperforms the self-supervised baselines and yields more robust and discriminative representations.
papers.comment: 31 pages, including supplementary material; 3 figures and 2 tables

papers.title: Graphical Models Induced by Irreversible Event Accumulation on Trees
papers.summary: Decomposable graphical models are usually adopted for their computational convenience rather than derived from a data-generating mechanism. We show that a special class of them arises naturally from the irreversible accumulation of events along a branching history. Each event is attached to an edge of a latent rooted tree and is inherited by everything below that edge; an observation records which events have occurred at a randomly chosen node, not necessarily a leaf. When the tree is a path, this is the cumulative coding of an ordinal variable, whose indicators form a Markov chain; in the general tree case the Markov chain is replaced by a junction tree. The conditional independence graph of the event indicators is always decomposable and, in fact, is the line graph of the tree (maximal cliques correspond to nodes where two or more edges meet and separators are the single events on the edges joining two such nodes). The graph determines the tree up to the choice of root. A connected graph arises in this way if, and only if, it is chordal, any two of its maximal cliques share at most one vertex, no vertex is in three maximal cliques, and the graph is such that any two maximal cliques share at most one vertex. This provides a simple graphical test for compatibility with the mechanism (necessary but not sufficient, as irreversibility also constrains the distribution's support). The structure breaks down if we look at just the leaves, and measurement error destroys the exact screening and leads to a denser graph rather than simply a weaker dependence. We discuss inference, provide diagnostics for departures such as recurrent events, illustrate them on some simulated data and discuss their application in the context of mutation accumulation and lineage tracing where both ancestral and descendant types are sampled together.

papers.title: Graphical Modeling from Marginal Information via Optimal Transport
papers.summary: A graphical model represents multivariate interactions through conditional independence, but requires jointly observed samples to be fitted to data. When individuals cannot be tracked and only marginal observations are available, as with destructive measurements leading to cross-sectional data, the problem of graphical modeling is confounded with that of assembling a joint law. We show how simultaneous graphical modeling and joint law assembly can be realized via a multi-marginal optimal transport problem with graphical cost. Focusing on Gaussian marginals, we generate a joint law satisfying the Markov properties prescribed by a given graph. Within the class of joint distributions respecting the graph and marginals constraints, our construction selects a member by making the interactions set by the graph as strong as possible under a dependence budget measured by relative entropy. In the empirical setting, where only estimates of the marginals are available, we examine the stability of the problem under perturbations of both the marginals and of the graph weights. The resulting error splits into an estimation term, vanishing with the sample size, and a specification term, which quantifies the cost of a misspecified graph. Finally, we illustrate these findings by numerical experiments.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Under Runtime Confounding: Policy Learning and Off-Policy Evaluation
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to train robust, adaptable systems across healthcare, e-commerce, and robotics. In these settings, legal, ethical, or logistical concerns may preclude certain key variables that drive decisions from being collected during deployment time. This gives rise to a setting known as runtime confounding: the logged data hold full observability, but deployment time lacks knowledge of certain variables, known as runtime confounders. Unlike single timepoint and non-adaptive settings, runtime confounding under reinforcement learning has the potential to propagate over time, as earlier decisions affect future states, observations, and action assignments, leading to biased learning. We address these problems with three contributions: we (1) develop policy learning algorithms under runtime-confounding, (2) develop semi-parametric efficient off-policy estimation procedures, and (3) provide diagnostics for understanding the price of runtime confounding.

papers.title: Adaptive Sequential Surveillance of Infectious Diseases Under Limited Sampling Capacity
papers.summary: This paper develops a closed-loop adaptive sequential surveillance framework for infectious disease monitoring with limited surveillance resources. In this framework, we use a Bayesian spatio-temporal model to predict disease prevalence at each location, and propose several adaptive site-allocation strategies based on the posterior probabilities that the predictions exceed a predefined threshold. These strategies exploit high-risk locations while also exploring, by random or recency-based sampling or by incorporating the frontiers of emerging outbreaks. To address the unequal inclusion probabilities induced by adaptive sampling, we integrate inverse-probability weighting (IPW) into each model update. A simulation study showed that adaptive surveillance strategies improved outbreak detection relative to uniform sampling and fixed sentinel sampling. Frontier-based strategies improved detection and timeliness relative to risk-proportional allocation. When IPW was used to update the model, some proposed strategies yielded lower inferential bias compared with the standard unweighted update, particularly for strategies that allowed more flexible exploration. Credible-interval coverage varied by strategy. The results identify trade-offs between exploitation of known high-risk locations and exploration of potential outbreak frontiers.
papers.comment: The abstract of this project has been accepted for poster presentation at the Royal Statistical Society 2026 International Conference

papers.title: Sequince: a modular sequential Monte Carlo toolkit
papers.summary: Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods approximate sequences of probability distributions using populations of weighted samples and are widely applicable, including in Bayesian inference and particle filtering. We present sequince, a modular Python toolkit for constructing SMC algorithms from reusable and extensible components. The toolkit provides modular steps for weighting, resampling, mutation, transformation, and control operations that are composed to implement different algorithms. It also includes prebuilt samplers for tempered SMC, persistent sampling and nested sampling via SMC. Its core components follow the Python Array API standard, supporting NumPy, JAX, PyTorch, and CuPy, enabling analyses on CPUs or GPUs. Random-number control and checkpointing support reproducible scientific workflows. This paper describes sequince v0.1.0 and its design as reusable infrastructure for methodological research and application of SMC methods.

papers.title: Outcome-dependent density combination by mixture Bayesian predictive synthesis
papers.summary: In the problem of density combination, the decision maker receives multiple density functions and is tasked to learn which density is used most in which region of the outcome space, and to combine them into a single density. The outcome-dependent density combination can be cast as the Bayesian predictive synthesis, where the decision maker's uncertainty is naturally integrated. The models for the outcome-dependent weights have been considered in Johnson and West (2025), but limited to the Gaussian density kernel. In this study, we point out the limitation of the model flexibility of the Gaussian weights, and theoretically and numerically verify that the estimated weights can be least outcome-dependent. As an alternative, we propose the use of the softmax (logistic-normal) functions as the models for the weights, together with the bias-adjustment to the submitted densities. The posterior computation is feasible by using the custom Metropolis-Hastings method with the Pólya-gamma augmentation. The utility of the proposed method is illustrated in the real data analysis of movie theatre revenues, where a human expert reports the point quantile forecasts without any uncertainty quantification.

papers.title: Probabilistic Meshless Methods on Manifolds
papers.summary: Probabilistic meshless methods solve partial differential equations (PDEs) by placing a Gaussian process prior on the solution and conditioning it on the PDE at a finite set of collocation nodes. The posterior provides both an approximation of the solution and a Bayesian quantification of its error. While these methods are well established on Euclidean domains, their extension to manifolds lacks, to our knowledge, any convergence analysis. We extend them to compact manifolds and study their convergence in two settings. First, for known manifolds whose Laplace-Beltrami eigenpairs are available, the prior can be evaluated exactly, but the PDE operator generally cannot be applied to it in closed form. We replace this operator by a standard generalized finite difference discretization on a point cloud sampled from the manifold, and show that the resulting method is consistent at the points of the cloud, at a rate governed by their fill distance. Second, for implicit manifolds, known only through a point cloud, both the prior and the operator must be approximated. We propose a new generalized finite difference scheme with a free stencil radius, and show that it retains the consistency of the standard construction while controlling the growth of its coefficients, and that an appropriate radius yields uniform convergence of the discrete Gram matrix. In both settings, we derive error bounds for the posterior mean which separate the collocation error intrinsic to the method from the error due to approximating the operator and, for implicit manifolds, the prior. Experiments on the circle, the sphere and the flat torus confirm our theoretical claims. On real-world cortical thickness data, our approach attains the accuracy of established discretizations, while conditioning on fewer than a tenth of the observations and providing a credible interval at every vertex.

papers.title: Reference-based multiple imputation for longitudinal bounded discrete outcomes
papers.summary: Reference-based multiple imputation has been developed for binary and ordinal responses. We develop a parsimonious formulation for longitudinal bounded scores and counts that preserves their finite integer support and gives partial and complete reference borrowing an explicit distributional interpretation. Discrete Kumaraswamy margins provide closed-form cumulative distribution and quantile functions, simplifying fitting and imputation under a Gaussian copula. Borrowing is defined through a regression model indexed by a smooth median anchor, allowing continuation under the assigned treatment, partial borrowing, or jump to reference after a specified trigger. With shapes shared across arms, complete borrowing replaces the active marginal distribution with the reference distribution at the same visit and covariate values, while conditional imputations remain informed by retained outcomes. Bayesian estimation uses latent variable augmentation, and all sensitivity rules share one fitted posterior. Completed datasets are analyzed using a beta-binomial random intercept model, with treatment comparisons expressed as standardized mean score differences. Simulations assess parameter recovery and imputation followed by analysis. An application to depression scores illustrates attenuation of the treatment benefit at the final visit as borrowing increases, with confidence intervals including zero under all rules.

papers.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Blind Passive Beamforming in RIS-Assisted MIMO Systems
papers.summary: Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) are a promising solution for improving millimeter-wave (mmWave) communications by controlling signal propagation. Yet, selecting the optimal RIS configuration remains challenging due to the high-dimensional search space and signaling overhead. We propose a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) framework for blind passive beamforming, where a Deep Q-Learning (DQL) agent learns an adaptive policy to select near-optimal RIS configurations while sounding only few codewords, without channel state information. Results show that our approach outperforms Q-Learning (QL) and conventional baselines in convergence, performance, and overhead reduction.
papers.comment: Accepted at AIxNET 2026. 6 pages. Copyright may be transferred to IEEE after publication, after which this version may no longer be accessible

papers.title: Bayes-Consistent Losses for Adaptive Inference in Classification
papers.summary: Adaptive inference systems balance accuracy and inference cost by routing inputs to models with varying capabilities. Although jointly training models and routers is empirically more sample-efficient than training them separately, principled losses for joint training remain underexplored. We address this gap in a classification setting by proposing cost-sensitive hinge losses for jointly training classifiers with single-stage or cascade routers. Single-stage routers directly select a model per input, whereas cascade routers sequentially decide at each stage whether to predict with the current model or defer to the next stage, which uses a more accurate but more costly model. For both settings, we prove linear calibration bounds establishing Bayes consistency: minimizing the hinge risk recovers the Bayes-optimal risk under the target cost-sensitive zero-one loss. Moreover, since routers can require more labeled data to train than classifiers, we propose a novel post-training prediction-powered inference (PPI) procedure that uses unlabeled data to refine a trained single-stage router. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that the proposed hinge losses are effective for joint training and that PPI can correct routing errors when labeled data is scarce.

papers.title: Confidence Filtering in Video-Based Gait Assessment: Measurement Error versus Selection Shift
papers.summary: Video-based gait assessment often keeps only high-confidence pose observations, which can lower measurement error but change the movement assessed. We compared confidence selection with budget-matched random selection in a Parkinson-related cohort (n = 96) and an NF2-related replication cohort (n = 18). In the Parkinson-related cohort, confidence selection produced a small but consistent shift in the observed movement summary (+0.05 SD, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.07), while held-out Mini-BESTest error stayed flat (-0.04 points, -0.13 to 0.05); a policy preserving motion-group proportions reduced the shift, while NF2 showed no shift and its predictor did not beat a constant baseline. Because this shift mixes measurement error with selection shift, we decompose and simulate both on the cohort's window structure. Filtering lowers local error when error depends on confidence, but biases the endpoint once confidence tracks movement more than error. In the Parkinson-related data, confidence was only weakly tied to movement (rho = 0.14). There, filtering is harmless if well-tracked windows are unbiased. If instead systematic error only redistributes within participants, filtering can add up to 0.58 degrees. Unchanged clinical error from such small-cohort predictors therefore cannot show that quality filtering preserves the assessed movement.

papers.title: Generalized Posterior Calibration via Infinitesimal-Jackknife Variance Matching
papers.summary: Generalized posteriors update a prior through an exponential transformation of empirical loss rather than a conventional likelihood, with a learning rate controlling posterior concentration. Their credible intervals may have incorrect frequentist coverage because posterior dispersion need not reflect sampling variability. We propose infinitesimal-jackknife variance matching (IJVM), a computationally efficient method for selecting the learning rate for a prespecified scalar functional. IJVM matches the functional's posterior variance to an infinitesimal-jackknife estimate of the sampling variance of its posterior mean, computed from posterior covariances with observation-level losses. A multiplicative one-step update requires one pilot posterior fit and a second fit for inference, avoiding explicit estimation of loss Hessians or gradient covariance matrices and repeated bootstrap posterior fitting. Under suitable regularity and Monte Carlo accuracy conditions, we establish consistency of the selected rate for the functional-specific first-order calibration target. With additional sampling and posterior-quantile assumptions, the resulting credible intervals achieve asymptotically nominal frequentist coverage. Simulations involving homoscedastic and heteroscedastic regression and hinge-loss classification show that one-step IJVM achieves coverage near the nominal 95% level, with interval lengths comparable to bootstrap-based generalized posterior calibration but substantially fewer posterior fits. Additional updates offer little improvement.

papers.title: Variational Bayes for Variable Selection with Adaptive Sharing across Populations and Responses
papers.summary: We propose a variational Bayesian framework for variable selection with multiple responses across heterogeneous populations. The prior dependence among the inclusion indicators allows variable-selection information to be shared at different levels across populations and responses, while regression coefficients remain population- and response-specific. When the appropriate sharing structure is unknown, a data-driven rule adaptively determines the scope of information sharing from marginal association evidence. The resulting variational algorithm is computationally scalable and can be implemented using either individual-level or summary data. Under regularity conditions, we establish selection consistency and convergence properties of the variational parameters at fixed iterations of the algorithm for fixed dimension case. In high dimensions, we establish model-selection consistency and coefficient contraction in both $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ norms. Simulation studies show competitive variable selection performance and demonstrate the potential gains from joint analysis. We further illustrate the summary-data implementation using genome-wide association summary statistics from the 2021 Global Lipids Genetics Consortium study for four lipid traits across five populations.
papers.comment: 18 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Supplementary material (54 pages) is available as an ancillary PDF

papers.title: Formalizing the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes by a Generalized Notion of Co-dimension
papers.summary: In this work, we formalize the concept of intrinsic dimension of objective landscapes introduced in Li et al. (2018), which measures the structural complexity of learning problems by training along randomly generated subspaces. We define the intrinsic dimension of a set $Θ\subset\mathbb{R}^p$ as the minimal dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}(Θ)$ such that a random plane of dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}(Θ)$ in $\mathbb{R}^p$ intersects $Θ$ with probability one. We show that it is a generalized notion of co-dimension that depends on the global geometry of $Θ$. We study mathematical properties of the intrinsic dimension and develop techniques to estimate the intrinsic dimension of sets $Θ$ that arise in learning problems. More specifically, we derive upper and/or lower bounds where $Θ$ is the set of optimal parameters in student-teacher settings with shallow and deep ReLU networks, including finite and infinite sample cases, and with and without regularization. We discuss how our theory leads to novel types of generalization bounds, thereby showing that the intrinsic dimension is a measure of learning complexity. Our results connect techniques from seemingly different areas of machine learning research such as classification of symmetries of ReLU networks and stochastic geometry.
